text: ← Advanced contents AVAILABLE CHAPTERS WHAT YOU WILL LEARNCompute Compton y from scattering probability and electron temperature, derive the thermal SZ frequency dependence, and explain what the signal measures about cluster electron pressure. Connect to foundations: The classical electron radius and Thomson scattering ↗ Compare solution assumptions and boundary data in the solution library ↗ 01Use background light to measure a galaxy cluster The cosmic microwave background (CMB) has a nearly blackbody spectrum at 2.7255 K. Hot, diffuse gas fills the space between galaxies in a cluster. Its free electrons scatter passing CMB photons, which on average gain energy through inverse Compton scattering. The resulting small spectral distortion in the cluster direction is the thermal Sunyaev–Zel’dovich (SZ) effect. Thermal SZ is driven by random electron motion. Kinetic SZ, due to the cluster’s bulk line-of-sight motion, is introduced separately in the final extension. This chapter focuses on the connection between cluster gas and observables, taking the scattering collision operator as a physical input. 02Gain per scattering and scattering probability Let ε be photon energy and Te electron temperature. Use nonrelativistic electrons and the Thomson limit: photon energy in the electron rest frame is much smaller than mec². For isotropic photons and electrons, averaging to second order in electron speed gives fractional energy gain (4/3)⟨v²/c²⟩. ⟨v²⟩ = 3kBTeme ⟨Δεε⟩ ≈ 43⟨v²⟩c² = 4θe, θe ≡ kBTemec² The factor 4/3 comes from averaging scattering geometry and Doppler shifts. The recoil term −ε/(mec²) is negligible for CMB photons scattering on hot cluster electrons. The result 4θe is a mean gain per scattering, not the complete SZ spectral shape. For a uniform electron density ne and line-of-sight depth L, the scattering optical depth is τ = neσTL. The probability of at least one scattering is 1 − e−τ, approximately τ when τ ≪ 1. τ = neσTL, y ≡ τθe Mean photon energy gainInitial energy ≈ 4y The final line estimates the ensemble mean energy gain to first order, not the brightness change at every frequency. 03y adds electron pressure along the line of sight If density and temperature vary along the path, add contributions dy = θe neσT dl. Introducing ideal-gas electron pressure Pe = nekBTe makes the observable explicit. y = ∫ kBTemec²neσTdl = σTmec²∫ Pedl σT is an area and Pe dl has units of energy per area, so y is dimensionless. Pe is electron pressure, distinct from total gas pressure including ions. At constant temperature y/τ gives θe, but a thermal SZ signal alone does not separately determine τ and Te. kBTe = 8 keV, ne = 10−3 cm−3, L = 1 Mpc τ ≈ 2.05×10−3, θe ≈ 8511, y ≈ 3.21×10−5 A temperature quoted in keV denotes the thermal energy kBTe. Eight keV corresponds to about 9.3×10⁷ K. Use 1 cm⁻³ = 10⁶ m⁻³ and 1 Mpc ≈ 3.086×10²² m. 04Calculate a distortion of the Planck spectrum Write CMB temperature as T₀ and frequency as ν, and define x = hν/(kBT₀). Express the Planck spectrum using photon occupation N₀ and intensity scale I₀. N₀ is distinct from electron number density ne. N₀(x) = 1ex−1, Bν = I₀x³N₀(x) I₀ = 2(kBT₀)³h²c² For hot nonrelativistic electrons, τ ≪ 1, and y ≪ 1, take the following first-order consequence of the Kompaneets scattering equation as input. It represents repeated small energy changes as diffusion in frequency space. ΔN ≈ yx²ddx(x⁴dN₀dx) Insert dN₀/dx = −eˣ/(eˣ−1)². Apply the product rule to x⁴ and the exponential term, then use ΔIν = I₀x³ΔN. Collecting terms exposes the bracket that controls the sign. ΔIν = I₀y x⁴ex(ex−1)² f(x) f(x) ≡ xex+1ex−1−4 This is a leading nonrelativistic result, not a full relativistic scattering solution. The panel displays the small difference ΔIν. A small-y expansion should not be used to manufacture an exaggerated, highly distorted full CMB spectrum. 05The low-frequency deficit and the approximately 217 GHz null For x ≪ 1, eˣ ≈ 1+x and x(eˣ+1)/(eˣ−1) tends to two. Thus f(x) tends to −2: a low-frequency deficit. Photons have gained energy and been redistributed toward higher frequencies. Brightness differences are often expressed as the temperature change that would produce them in a blackbody. Linearize ΔIν = (∂Bν/∂T)ΔT and differentiate the Planck function: ∂Bν∂T = I₀T₀x⁴ex(ex−1)² ΔTthT₀ = yf(x) → −2y (x ≪ 1) This is a frequency-dependent conversion to CMB thermodynamic temperature, not a claim that the distorted spectrum is a blackbody at a different single temperature. Solving f(x) = 0 gives x ≈ 3.830, or ν ≈ 217.5 GHz at T₀ = 2.7255 K. The thermal signal changes sign across this null. The panel uses the leading nonrelativistic formula, so changing electron temperature does not move its thermal null. Relativistic corrections change the spectral shape and null in reality. Precision analysis of hot clusters requires more than this approximation. 06What does this tell us about a cluster? Measuring y across the sky gives a map of line-of-sight electron pressure. Combine it with other temperature and density measurements to study hot intracluster gas. A pressure-column measurement is not by itself a direct measurement of total cluster mass. The first-order thermal spectrum cannot distinguish hotter, lower-density gas from cooler, denser gas with the same y. Multiple frequencies help isolate its sign-changing spectrum, while dust emission, radio sources, and primary CMB fluctuations must also be considered. 07Extension: distinguish kinetic SZ Bulk motion of cluster gas relative to the CMB creates a Doppler signal distinct from random thermal motion. Take v_∥ positive away from the observer, with small optical depth and |v_∥| ≪ c. ΔTkinT₀ ≈ −τv∥c Receding gas gives a negative signal and approaching gas a positive one. At this order the thermodynamic-temperature shift is independent of frequency and has no thermal-style sign reversal near 217 GHz. The intensity difference still depends on frequency through ∂Bν/∂T. Selecting a velocity in the panel adds kinetic SZ to the thermal intensity difference. For example, τ ≈ 0.00205 and v_∥ = 300 km/s give ΔTkin ≈ −5.60 μK. Kinetic SZ and other emission can remain at the thermal null, so 217 GHz does not isolate the unmodified background. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. In a uniform slab, double the electron temperature, halve its density, and keep its depth fixed. How do τ and y change? Can the first-order nonrelativistic thermal SZ spectra distinguish these cases? What about kinetic SZ? Show the answer and reasoning τ = neσTL halves, while y = τkBTe/(mec²) stays fixed. The first-order thermal spectra used here are identical, so temperature and density cannot be separated. At fixed line-of-sight speed, kinetic SZ halves because it is proportional to τ. Relativistic corrections can carry extra temperature information; this degeneracy belongs to the stated approximation.
